paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Metamorphism is what happens when an existing rock is changed into a rock with different minerals or a different texture. The starting rock is called the protolith. The change usually happens above 150 °C, often with raised pressure or with chemically active fluids present. Through all of it the rock stays mostly solid: it is transformed without melting to any great degree.

paragraphs.heading: Where it starts and stops
paragraphs.text: Metamorphism is not the same as weathering or diagenesis, which are changes at or just beneath Earth's surface. It is generally taken to begin at 100 to 200 °C. That leaves out the compaction and lithification that produce sedimentary rocks. The upper limit is the solidus, the temperature at which the rock begins to melt. Past that point the process counts as igneous instead.

paragraphs.heading: How solid rock can change
paragraphs.text: A rock can change without melting because heat breaks the bonds between atoms. The freed atoms move and bond with other atoms. Fluid in the pores between mineral grains is an important medium for this exchange of atoms. Existing minerals can then recrystallize, or new minerals can crystallize with different crystal structures or chemical compositions. The minerals of the protolith end up in forms that are more stable under the pressure and temperature where the change takes place.

paragraphs.heading: Recrystallization
paragraphs.text: Recrystallization is the change in the size and orientation of grains in a rock during metamorphism. The mineral keeps its identity; only its texture changes. Limestone and chalk hold small calcite crystals, and these become larger crystals in marble, a metamorphic rock. In sandstone, the original quartz sand grains recrystallize into quartzite, a very compact rock of interlocked quartz crystals. Both high temperature and high pressure contribute.

paragraphs.heading: Why crystals grow coarser
paragraphs.text: Metamorphic rocks are typically more coarsely crystalline than their protolith. Atoms inside a crystal are surrounded by a stable arrangement of neighbours. At the surface that arrangement is partly missing, which produces a surface energy and makes the surface unstable. Growing into coarser crystals reduces the surface area and so minimizes that energy. Rock that is intensely deformed can go the other way, shedding its strain energy as it recrystallizes into mylonite, a rock with fine grains.

paragraphs.heading: An experiment in a cannon barrel
paragraphs.text: James Hutton, a Scottish naturalist, was the first to recognize how important heating is in forming metamorphic rock. In 1795 he wrote that some rock beds of the Scottish Highlands had once been sedimentary rock and had been transformed by great heat. He also speculated that pressure mattered. His friend James Hall tested the idea by sealing chalk in a makeshift pressure vessel built from a cannon barrel and heating it in an iron foundry furnace. The result strongly resembled marble, not the quicklime that chalk usually gives when heated in open air.
